item.title: Rigid-Container Gas Data: Zero-Pressure Temperature and Moles
item.stimulus:
A fixed amount of an ideal gas is sealed in a rigid container of volume 4.0 × 10⁻³ m³. A student measures the gas pressure at several temperatures:
T (°C) | P (kPa)
20 | 120.0
50 | 132.3
80 | 144.6
110 | 156.9

Use R = 8.31 J/(mol·K) and T(K) = T(°C) + 273.

parts.prompt: Using the data, determine the temperature, in degrees Celsius, at which the pressure of the gas would be zero if the trend in the data continued.

criteria.text: Finds about −273 °C by extending the linear trend (slope 0.41 kPa per °C) to zero pressure.
criteria.evidence: Response finds the pressure rises by 12.3 kPa per 30 °C (0.41 kPa/°C) and extrapolates from a data point to P = 0, getting a value between −276 °C and −270 °C.
criteria.fix: Find the constant change in P per degree, then work backward from a data point until the pressure reaches zero.

parts.prompt: Calculate the number of moles of gas in the container.

criteria.text: Calculates n = PV/(RT) ≈ 0.197 mol, using P = 1.200 × 10⁵ Pa and T = 293 K.
criteria.evidence: Response converts 120.0 kPa to pascals and 20 °C to 293 K before substituting into PV = nRT, obtaining about 0.197 mol (or uses another row consistently).
criteria.fix: In PV = nRT, always use pressure in pascals and absolute temperature in kelvins before substituting.

parts.prompt: All of the gas is moved into a different container with half the volume, and it is heated until its absolute temperature is twice its absolute temperature at 20 °C. No gas escapes. Determine the new pressure of the gas.

criteria.text: Finds the pressure increases by a factor of 4, to 480 kPa, because P = nRT/V with n constant, T doubled, and V halved.
criteria.evidence: Response uses the ideal gas law with n fixed to combine a factor of 2 from temperature and a factor of 2 from volume, giving 4 × 120.0 kPa = 480 kPa.
criteria.fix: Write P = nRT/V and apply each change as a factor: doubling T doubles P, and halving V doubles P again.

parts.prompt: The ideal-gas model becomes less accurate when a gas is compressed into a very small volume. Identify one assumption of the ideal-gas model that fails under these conditions and explain why it fails.

criteria.text: Identifies a relevant assumption and explains its failure: the atoms' own volume is no longer negligible compared with the container volume, or the atoms are close enough that forces between them other than during collisions become appreciable.
criteria.evidence: Response names one of these two assumptions and connects its failure to the atoms being packed closely together in a small volume.
criteria.fix: Recall the model's assumptions (negligible atomic volume, forces only during collisions) and ask which depend on atoms being far apart.

item.model_answer:
(a) Each 30 °C increase raises the pressure by 12.3 kPa, so the pressure is linear in temperature with slope 12.3/30 = 0.41 kPa/°C. Starting at 20 °C and 120.0 kPa, the pressure reaches zero after a decrease of 120.0/0.41 ≈ 293 °C, at T ≈ 20 − 293 ≈ −273 °C.

(b) P = 120.0 kPa = 1.200 × 10⁵ Pa, T = 20 + 273 = 293 K.
n = PV/(RT) = (1.200 × 10⁵ Pa)(4.0 × 10⁻³ m³)/[(8.31 J/(mol·K))(293 K)] = 480/2435 ≈ 0.197 mol.

(c) From PV = nRT, P = nRT/V. The amount of gas n is constant. T doubles, which doubles P, and V is halved, which doubles P again. P_new = 2 × 2 × 120.0 kPa = 480 kPa.

(d) The model assumes the volume of the atoms is negligible compared with the volume occupied by the gas. When the gas is squeezed into a very small volume, the atoms take up a significant fraction of that volume, so this assumption fails. (Also acceptable: the model assumes the only appreciable forces act during collisions, but when atoms are packed close together the forces between them at other times are no longer negligible.)
